utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed that there was one short preliminary matter to be raised by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Thank you. The Prosecution has received a revised English translation for P470, which was originally 65 ter 03687. The document was admitted through Witness Dorothea Hanson on 7 November 2012 and was used again with Witness Mijanovic on 25 November 2014, when an issue arose regarding the translation. See transcript 28830 to 28834, specifically T28833. The revised translation has been uploaded into e-court under doc ID 022374700-ET. It appears the Defence has no objection to the revised translation, so we would request that the court officer be instructed to replace the current translation with the revised version. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Bibles. The Chamber was copied on an e-mail sent by Mr. Djurdjevic to Ms. Stewart that the Defence has objection to the revised English translation. Therefore, Madam Registrar, you are instructed to replace the existing translation by the one newly provided under the number as just mentioned by Ms. Bibles. And that's it. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bilbija.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Ivetic will now continue his examination-in-chief. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to start off where we left off, and I'd like to call up D832 and I'd like to look at page 8 in both languages and paragraph 9 of your written statement. In paragraph 9, sir, you talk of the medical treatment for a little girl from Gorazde. What role, if any, did General Mladic and the VRS Main Staff play in this event?

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I remember. In this case, General Mladic's role was manifested, as far as I can remember, at the moment when the girl's treatment was already over; that is to say, she stayed in hospital even once her medical treatment was completed. As for the role of General Mladic, it had to do with the moment when the girl was supposed to be returned to her parents. So there were several contacts between the hospital and the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, until finally this return was organised - I don't remember exactly when or how that happened. I just remember that we said good-bye to the girl because she had really become everyone's pet at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could stay on the same page in the Serbian and go to the next page in the English, I'd like to look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- could you establish a time-frame for this episode.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Doctor, do you recall what the time-frame was for this incident involving Minka Zivojevic of Gorazde, at least a year?

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was 1992. I don't remember exactly. I cannot remember the date when this occurred. I think it was summertime.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you recall for approximately how long this individual had stayed at the hospital after her initial treatment?

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'd say perhaps even longer than a month, because the girl was already doing fine but she just stayed there and became friends with everybody at the hospital. The nurses were very kind to her because there weren't really any other children there. She was staying at the ward where I worked, so in a way this little girl became attached to me as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now if we could turn to the next page in the English, I'd like to look at paragraph 11 of your statement. And here you talk about what you saw from the helicopter, these fires. What exactly did you learn about who had started the fires and for what reason?

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly? Are we speaking about the night, the night, Srebrenica, flying?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, we are.

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That night the General personally ordered me to go to Srebrenica where something had happened. A Canadian soldier, when the garbage was being burned, he set his own uniform on fire and sustained burns in that way. Two helicopters came to pick me up at the football stadium in Sokolac and I went to Srebrenica that way. From the helicopter we saw fire in several places. It was about 11.00 in the evening. We saw several fires in the dark. I asked the soldiers in the helicopter what all of that was, and they told me that these were fires that the population of Srebrenica were starting on hilltops so that aircraft throwing packages of humanitarian aid could orientate themselves and know where they should drop them from these planes. When we landed at the football stadium in Srebrenica, I think we exchanged a few words on that topic there as well and got the same answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That soldier who had suffered the burns had already received first aid and had already been taken care of in that way. So he was just put into the helicopter and we returned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, same question: Time-frame? And could you also further explore with whom he had a conversation when he had landed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Doctor, you've heard the comments of the Presiding Judge. Could you offer any assistance as to the time-frame?

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was in the autumn of 1992. Now the conversation at the stadium, who it took place with, again these were uniformed men from UNPROFOR. I don't remember there was anyone there who spoke Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'd like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What was then the language you used for your conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'd now like to look at paragraphs 16 through 17 on page 4 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Here you discuss a medivac evacuation of persons from Srebrenica. First I want to ask you: Were these persons civilians or soldiers that were being evacuated?

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for this evacuation from Srebrenica, everyone wore civilian clothing, but some of the persons who had boarded the helicopter were wounded persons and these wounds had been sustained quite a while ago. So their medical treatment had already been well underway. They themselves said that they were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And in relation to the order that you received from General Mladic in relation to participating in this medevac as indicated at the last sentence in paragraph 17, were such types of orders from General Mladic, were they out of the ordinary? Extraordinary?

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic sometimes, rarely, was in a position to issue orders to me directly as regards our work. He never missed the opportunity to underline the following to us: That we should strictly behave in accordance with the rules of our profession and that we should take good care, if it has to do with the wounded of the other side or civilians, et cetera, persons of a different religion and so on, that no one should feel that they have not been given full treatment or full attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And lastly, Doctor, this medevac operation from Srebrenica in April of 1993, approximately how many persons were evacuated in the course of that operation?

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The evacuation took place with two helicopters. A large number of people boarded these helicopters. We knew that exactly then, I don't know exactly, but I think about 20 people could be taken in a single helicopter. They took these people to Tuzla, and during that time we would be waiting there and during the day I think there would be four trips.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor, for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that completes the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Before I give an opportunity to Mr. Zec to cross-examine the witness, could you tell us, you said four trips, 20 people on board of a helicopter. Were all of those 80, were they all soldiers or were some of them soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just some of them were soldiers and I would say a smaller number at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have a question too. Were these four trips by each helicopter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Four times for both helicopters because they fly together, in pairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So there would be about 160 people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would say that that would be an appropriate estimate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- remembering all the people who were waiting there and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I thank my colleague for correcting my having ignored that there were two helicopters rather than one. His math is better than mine. Mr. Zec, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bilbija, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Zec, you'll find him to your right. Mr. Zec is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And good morning, Mr. Bilbija.

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: You told us in your statement about your employment before the war. At this time, Mr. Bilbija, you were a reserve officer in the JNA with the rank of captain; correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In paragraph 7 you say you transferred to Sokolac at the end of May 1992 and that you were admitted into active military service with the rank of major. As of 1992, you were active officer within VJ, the Yugoslav army; correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And your service with VJ was terminated in 1998. At that time you held the rank of lieutenant-colonel; correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In paragraph 6 you talk about your discussions with General Mladic regarding your deployment to Benkovac and then you say you went to Sipo in 1992. So in April 1992 when you moved to Bosnia, you discussed with General Mladic transport of weapons; correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: You already told us in your statement about your discussions with General Mladic regarding your deployment to Benkovac and then you said in April 1992 you went to Sipo during the Kupres operations. So my question is: When you talked to General Mladic in April 1992, you discussed with him transport of weapons; correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall such a conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have P352 and we need page 163 in both languages. And for the B/C/S version we will need transcript of the notebook, not the handwritten version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Bilbija, in front of you -- on the screen in front of you it's coming, it's a notebook of General Mladic. And we will be looking at the entry dated 3 April 1992. And it says: "Dr. Simo Bilbija: "I expected you to call me concerning the vehicle given for transport of weapons." So this was what you discussed with General Mladic; correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked to General Mladic many times. What you are showing me now doesn't jog my memory at all. I don't remember any of this, but what I do remember is that I always talked to him about medical matters, surgery, the treatment of wounded persons. I cannot recall what this is, this that you have been speaking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Well, having an opportunity to see this entry, does this refresh your memory about your discussions with General Mladic regarding transport of weapons?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zec, I think the witness answered the question already.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I'll move on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In paragraph 16, you say you were involved in evacuations of wounded from Srebrenica to Tuzla in April 1993. You did not provide any context, but this Chamber has received evidence about the events in the Eastern Bosnia in -- leading up to April 1993, including evidence about VRS combat operations in the area, forcing many civilians to flee towards Srebrenica. And in March 1993, many of these civilians held General Morillon, commander of UNPROFOR in Srebrenica, asking him for help and this was when General Morillon asked his headquarters to negotiate an agreement to take by helicopter those who were most seriously injured, to take them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And this can be found in P317, paragraphs 176 through 192.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Bilbija, were you aware of these events leading up to your involvement in the evacuations in April 1993?

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to repeat the question. Was I aware of -- informed about what was going on or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Yes, correct. Did you know -- were you aware about the events in the area of Eastern Bosnia, including Srebrenica, in the period leading up to your involvement in these evacuations in April 1993?

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of what was going on in the manner and to the extent of general information, public information. We knew that Srebrenica was in encirclement, we knew that negotiations were underway to find a solution for that situation. But as for the actual medevac action, I learned about it only at the point in time when I received an order to go there. Is that sufficient?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And during this period, including the period of the time of your visit, were you aware of the conditions in Srebrenica and that there was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue with that, could we more systematically go to what you put to the witness, Mr. Zec. Mr. Zec also mentioned VRS combat operations forcing many civilians to flee towards Srebrenica. Were you aware of that at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time I knew what we could find out from the media. There were no information -- there was no information that would be official information. That's something that I didn't receive about what was happening there. Better said, I was not aware of the details of the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you aware of VRS operations resulting in civilians fleeing to Srebrenica? Official, unofficial, media, were you aware of these things happening? And if so, by what source?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We knew but the source of information was mostly the news that was broadcast on TV.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you were aware of VRS combat operations resulting in civilians fleeing to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we knew that combat actions were going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bilbija, you are an intelligent man. Is there any reason why you leave out always half of what I ask you? I asked you about VRS operations resulting in civilians fleeing. And then you say: Yes, of course we were aware, we knew about operations. You leave out half of what I put to you. You did exactly the same with one of the previous questions of Mr. Zec. You confirm half of it and what -- another part which may be important as well, you just leave it out. Were you aware of VRS operations? You said "yes." Were you aware of that resulting in civilians fleeing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Why didn't you answer right in the beginning: I was aware of the operations, I learned from the media that it happened, but I was not aware of civilians fleeing? The answer is so simple from what I understand now. Mr. Zec, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Bilbija, you said you went to Srebrenica, and were you aware during the period before your trip to Srebrenica or the time when you were there about the conditions in town, that there was a growing number of civilians who were either killed or injured by VRS shelling of the town? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope that with my answer to this question I will also satisfy the Presiding Judge regarding the previous remarks regarding my answers. So we knew that combat actions were going on. As for the fact that a large number of civilians from the surrounding area had sought refuge in Srebrenica, that was something that we had just heard of from conversations amongst ourselves. Once I personally came to Srebrenica, then I could see for myself that the stories that we had heard were true. I saw many people there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you answered to one of the previous questions was: I knew that many civilians had gone to Srebrenica, where you just said that you were not aware of civilians fleeing to Srebrenica. Now, you've left out again part of the question. You are talking about combat operations. Were you aware of any shelling on the town of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot confirm that I knew that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, did you know it or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you permit me just to complete my answer to this question. Once I came to Srebrenica --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Bilbija, my question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness may complete his answer, as he requested.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the course of the day during the evacuation, I was with a young colleague of mine who had spent months in Srebrenica together with those civilians, treating the wounded, and I spoke with him in detail during the time the helicopters took to go to Tuzla and come back. So I asked him: How did you manage? What did you do? How did you do the surgeries? And it was a peer-to-peer kind of contact. During this conversation, the need arose for us to go to the hospital. It wasn't a need, actually, it was just collegial curiosity, his desire to show me where he was working. And as we were going to the hospital he showed me one place in the street where a shell had struck. So I saw a place where some sort of explosion left some sort of trail. He told me: See, look, this is where a shell fell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so you say shelling --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is how I found out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- one shell is the only thing you know that fell without any further details as when, but that's all you know about shelling of the town of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is what I saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you hear anything? Did he -- did someone tell you that it was not the only shell that fell, that many had fallen or that a few had fallen and when it was? Did you hear anything further?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When he showed me that, the colleague said that there had been several shells. We didn't really discuss that in detail. He said that there were a number of them in town and then we continued our conversation on a different topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Can we have 65 ter 12949.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Bilbija, coming on the screen will be UNPROFOR letter to Dr. Karadzic on 12 April 1993. It is in English but I'm going to read for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently the witness also understands English. Do you understand English? So therefore we leave it to you whether you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do understand it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we -- you can read what Mr. Zec says on the transcript which is on your screen. Mr. Zec, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And we need paragraph 1, which is on the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And paragraph 1 starts with: "Despite the promise of the pursuit of a political solution to the problem of Srebrenica, which I was given by General Mladic, I have received the following report from my people from Srebrenica ... "The latest casualty estimate in Srebrenica is 35 dead and 68 wounded but these are only those who had approached the hospital. MSF doctors report 10 of the wounded are likely to die in the next 24 hours. We believe there are other wounded in private homes and additional dead were not taken to hospital. "I personally have seen and counted 14 dead including 7 bodies on the road in front of the schoolhouse used as a refugee centre, where it appears most casualties occurred. 2 of the 7 bodies I saw in front of the hospital were children and one was decapitated." Paragraph 2, towards the end it says: "Even if there was some provocation of fire, this targeting of civilians is very hard to believe, let alone to ... justify." So, Mr. Bilbija, this incident and the shelling which also I believe you referred to earlier to Judge Orie's question, so were you aware of this shelling causing this many casualties during the course of one day in April 1993?

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 12949 receives number P6958, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Bilbija, during your visit to Srebrenica did you see or hear about hundreds and hundreds of people living on the street, having nowhere to go? Did you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my visit to Srebrenica, which lasted that whole day, we spent the time at the football-pitch where the triage was being carried out of those who were brought and transported to the pitch in order to be boarded to the helicopters. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Bilbija, people were living on the street, having nowhere to go. Did you see them while going to the health centre?

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is exactly what I was going to tell you. We went to the health centre and you could observe many people in town, but I couldn't get the impression that these people were living on the street. There were many people on the windows of the buildings which were immediately next to the football-pitch, where the process of boarding was going on. Once we came to the medical centre we saw people in the yard of the health centre. The doctor who was a local doctor who had brought me there introduced me to some of these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And in the health centre, did you see or did the doctor tell you about the conditions they were working in, no equipment, no water, no clean sheets, no space to put all the people who needed medical help? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me if I knew that before I came or whether I found that out when I arrived? What are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: When you were there and talking to the doctor.

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I wanted to say. He took me to visit and took me through the whole medical centre, introducing me to some members of the medical centre staff on the way. This was interesting for me to see, that's why we came, because I was interested in seeing it. I asked him to go there. I wanted to find out how he managed, what did he do, did he have the supplies. So he was explaining to me how he worked. Because during those few months - I don't know how long that period was that Srebrenica was encircled - he was the only doctor who was able to carry out any kind of surgical interventions. As far as his skill and training and technical and material capacities that were at his disposal in the medical centre --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I'm waiting now for approximately ten lines for you to answer the question: Did you find out about a lack of equipment, no water, no clean sheets, did you find out about that? And if Mr. Zec would like to know whether -- how you found out or whether there was sometimes water or not, he'll ask you. But was there a lack of supplies, equipment? Was there no water? Were there no clean sheets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that was the situation according to what the doctor said. He explained it more in terms of occasional shortage of water, shortage of medical supplies. I don't recall that we ever mentioned sheets. His medical centre, objectively speaking, and as far as my impression goes, it just looked like any medical centre on the other side, on my side. It was nothing special. He said that he received things from doctors from Doctors Without Borders. And that there was some supplies from humanitarian air-drops and that there was a depot of equipment, and then from that depot he gave me a present. He gave me a stethoscope.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I'm going now to show you a video of Srebrenica at the time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before we do that, can I just get clarification of something you talked about earlier. You talked of seeing many people on the windows. I'm not quite sure I understand what you mean by that. Could you please explain a little more what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I came to Srebrenica we knew that there was a large number of civilians there and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me stop you. Just what did you mean by "many people on the windows"? I know you saw many people when you came to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I wanted to say was that the evacuation from Srebrenica had attracted a lot of attention. People were curious. Some people were standing around the football-pitch and watching --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just let me stop you -- let me stop you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and then in the neighbouring buildings people were standing at the windows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. That's much better. Standing at the windows outside the buildings? If you can say in words rather than nod your head for the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were looking through the windows at the football-pitch, and you could see two or three persons at each of the windows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Through the windows. So they're inside the buildings, looking --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Inside the building, looking out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to show you a video of Srebrenica at the time, and perhaps you will be able to recognise some of the images.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: The video is 65 ter 22852A. The videotape has ERN number V000-7050-1-A. It is 6 minutes and 30 seconds long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have provided the B/C/S transcript -- translations of the video to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And we also have asked the CLSS to confirm the accuracy of the transcript, which they kindly did. So I suggest we play the video only once with the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is fine. Time-frame for the video, source of the video?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So the tape I identified, that is how long the tape is, 6 minutes and 30 seconds, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I mean with time-frame, when was it recorded, was it broadcasted? Is it a private recording? What is it we are looking at, apart from it being a video.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: It was a journalist who was in Srebrenica in the period late March/early April 1993 and he recorded that video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Tony Birtley: My first recollection is arriving at a village near Srebrenica just to be totally engulfed by hundreds and hundreds of people. I thought I was standing in a movie and I kept expecting somebody to say: Okay, cut. And all these people with these drawn, haunted faces, and they all got expressionless faces, it's like life had drained out of them. Life is ebbing away. There was very little caring by the so-called authorities following your arrival. Nobody cared for the refugees. They were left for days on the street. No one cared anything about them. They arrived, you know, we followed a family through and they had been walking for something like 17 hours. You know, the mother carrying a little boy who had been wounded by shrapnel in the hand. He had been wounded at the same time as his father. They came, they didn't know where they were going, they had no relatives and no friends. "Where does this man recommend they can sleep? Where does this man recommend they can go? "Unknown man: I don't know where. This town has 60.000 refugees and there's only room for 10.000. Have you seen how many people are sleeping on the street? "Tony Birtley: We helped them carry the sacks. I mean, it was a very, very small gesture, but this woman was toiling under two great sacks, and I must admit, I found one sack very difficult and she had two of them. And it struck me that I can't believe that these people, their people, and they didn't want to know. And then the father, he was treated in the hospital, and it was very tragic to see the little boy on the couch and the father on the couch and they'd both been wounded. And -- but actually, when treatment's finished, they're out because they can't have a space in the sought-after wards, because you can only have room for so many. And it was never intended to be a hospital, more a clinic. It's not a place where you can get the best possible treatment. And even the surgeon who I got to know quite well was very honest about that. You would come in there, you would have an operation very quickly. Your limb would come off, you would have your stomach sewn back in, shrapnel taken out as quickly as possible. If you were quite ill, you would stay in one of the wards and the wards are abysmal. "What the video cannot convey is the stench of unwashed sheets, unwashed bodies, of wounds becoming infected. I mean, they would always come and get -- they wanted to show me everything that was going on. Me, I was a way of telling the world the first time -- for the first time that everything they've said over ham radio is true. So whatever happened in the town they would say: 'Get Tony, get Tony.' And they'd call me into casualty. "All these little girls, there's about five or six little girls who've been hit by a shell and this little boy as well. And there was two screaming, although they had very small injuries. But there was the 10-year-old girl who was lying and she had, you know, what I've heard so many times in Srebrenica and Sarajevo as well, what they call the 'death look.' Her eyes are going blank. And they had been hit, they were out playing the south end of town. And later on we went to their home and one of them heard that her 4-year-old sister had been killed, she was killed instantly. And the mother was distraught and was weeping and wailing. And it -- like, you know, normal scenes, I think, in Bosnia. It's normality, that's the terrifying thing about it. "The medevac by helicopter was something that there was great uncertainty about, particularly by the Bosnian authorities. They didn't believe for one moment the Serbs would allow helicopters in and out of here, despite the fact that General Morillon was very, very confident. After the helicopters took off with their first batch of wounded, within, I don't know, two minutes, a shell. And it was artillery shell because you could hear that one coming in. You get a, shhhh, huge bang. "UN soldier: Roger. I have more incoming, more incoming. Over. "Tony Birtley: The majority of shrapnel sprayed to the south and that's why the two Canadian soldiers were wounded because they were further south. When this huge, confused scene was going on in the hospital of patching up the Canadian soldiers, lying quietly on a bench was this 5-year-old little boy who had been badly injured in a southern part of town in a separate incident by a Serbian mortar and it was hoped that he would be evacuated with the Canadian soldier. But as he went back down to the soccer field, the soccer field was shelled again. So the French colonel who had come in with the helicopters decided that there would be a medevac, but no landing on the soccer field, so they had to be winched up. But before the Canadian soldiers had been winched up, the baby had died in the arms of one of the Canadian soldiers. "It just seemed to me that it's a great injustice in some respects to these people that although we will put on helicopter flights when it's dangerous to evacuate UN soldiers, we're not prepared to do that for a 5-year-old boy who's an innocent victim. And it's a most tragic scene, you know, a father taking a little boy wrapped up in his golden plastic covering to keep him warm, sobbing uncontrollably, and his sobs and his weeping was drowned out by the blades of the helicopters as they winched up the Canadian soldiers and went off. And it seemed to sum up a lot about Srebrenica and Bosnia, that basically these people, you know, they come second."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Bilbija, this was the reality of Srebrenica and the conditions in which people were living there; correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This footage does not show that day when I was in Srebrenica, that is not that day. This could have been some other day. The day that I spent in Srebrenica was quiet, sunny, everything was going on in a planned manner as far as the transport was concerned. There were no incidents, there were no explosions. I wasn't -- I wasn't following whether the date of the film refers to that date. Is that what the film is trying to say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, if you say it was not on the day you were there, how do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I see in the footage -- actually, two Canadian soldiers who had been wounded are mentioned and there is this wounded child that is dying in his father's arms, but none of that could have happened without me knowing about it then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, I think that Mr. Zec asked primarily about the situation of people living on the streets, which was shown in the beginning of the footage. Could you please focus on that and tell us whether you consider it equally impossible that those shots were recorded on the day you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no doubt. I believe, actually, that it is impossible that this footage was taken on that day because the stadium and the medical centre are only a few hundred metres away from each other. The multitude of people, those scenes correspond to my memory. I already said that I saw a lot of people in the yard of the medical centre, but there were no explosions, especially not wounded UNPROFOR soldiers or this child, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first focus on the images you saw about people in the street. You said, well, you saw them in the courtyard of the hospital but what we saw on the video, whatever it is, seems not to be the courtyard of a hospital but seems to be a street in which people are more or less living; that is, they have fires, they have tables, they have chairs, sitting there, doing all kind of everyday activities. Let's focus on that first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is precisely what I've already answered, Mr. President. I saw a lot of people, but I did not see what I see in the footage here, those fires, all of that -- I mean, we've all seen it now, but I didn't see it then. It's true that we took this vehicle and went through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You just stop me, you don't want me to continue; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've answered the question what you saw on the footage was not what you saw at that point in time in town when you went from the stadium to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. I think we should take a break first, Mr. Zec. We take a break. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, you were speaking aloud. Did I hear you well that you mentioned the name of the Prosecutor who is cross-examining this witness? You may answer that question now. Did you use that name, speaking aloud? A yes or a no, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said "Zec." Zec is a last name in our parts and I asked the lawyer whether Mr. Zec --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, I just asked you --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You won't allow me to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I want you to answer my question and you have done so. You apparently have loudly spoken, pronouncing the name of Mr. Zec. We'll --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zec. I pronounced it Zec --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you now please -- please stop speaking. We'll consider -- we'll consider what the consequence of loudly pronouncing the name of the Prosecutor who is cross-examining the witness, what consequences that may have. You'll hear from us after the break. We'll take a break and we'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We don't have to wait until after the break. Could Mr. Mladic be removed from the courtroom until the end of the testimony of this witness because he continued to speak aloud when it was perfectly clear that not only in general terms he is not allowed to do so, but under the specific circumstances it's even more serious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break. Mr. Mladic is not to be taken into the courtroom after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bilbija, we'll continue. By the way, in the absence of Mr. Mladic we'll continue. Mr. Zec will now continue his cross-examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Bilbija, the shelling of the UNPROFOR that we saw on the video, that was one of the Serb attempts to obstruct the process of evacuations; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I object as to the foundation of the question. The witness has very clearly identified in detail that this was not the occasion that he was involved in, so I'd like to hear from the Prosecution as to their position that this is April of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I will reformulate my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Bilbija, were you aware of the Serb attempts to obstruct the process of evacuations?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will object as it is unspecific and generic and calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness may answer the question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Bilbija --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bilbija, could you please answer that question, whether you were aware of Serb attempts to obstruct the process of evacuations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I was not aware of such attempts because that part of the evacuation that I took part in myself proceeded in an unhindered fashion, and as I've already said, I had received orders from my superiors how to work, how to behave, and I've already spoken about that too. In addition to that, I was not the only person in that group of Serb officers who arrived in Srebrenica on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 09358. And this is a UN report about the events of 24 March 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Again, it will be in English but I will read for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: 65 ter 09358. And also there is a B/C/S translation of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In paragraph 1 it says: "The helicopter mission to evacuate wounded from Srebrenica was scheduled to begin at 0845 hrs local time on 24 March 93 following full clearance from Dr. Karadzic ..." Paragraph 2: "Tuzla airfield was shelled (15 impacts) ... but no damage to helicopters or injuries were sustained. The mission was confirmed ... at 0800 hrs and the first wave of Pumas flew to Zvornik for the agreed inspection of cargo. The Serb inspectors were totally obstructive ..." In paragraph 3 it says: "So that the process of -- that the evacuation should not fail because of these difficulties, the Landing Zone group were flown back to Tuzla in 2 lifts by one of the Pumas, while the remaining 3 aircraft now 'cleared' flew on to Srebrenica, arriving at ... 1130 ... at the same time 12 shells impacted in the area of the PTT building in Srebrenica ..." A few lines below: "The helicopters took off at 1158 ... and at 1203 hrs 4 rounds impacted ... followed shortly by a further 6 rounds which wounded 2 UN personnel (Canadian) and 1 civilian. One of the Canadians sustained serious head wounds." Paragraph 4, at the end it says: "Protests were lodged throughout the day to the Serb authorities on account of both the shelling and the deliberate contravention of the agreement by the inspectors at Zvornik." So this was the reality, Mr. Bilbija, the Serb side by obstructing the process of evacuation while the UNPROFOR was trying to enforce it. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honours. It's a compound question, mixing and matching facts from different incidents without clearly differentiating between the two. Again I ask: Is it the Prosecutor's position that this is the incident where the gentleman was involved in the medevac because in the statement it says April of 1993, and now we've dealt with two exhibits dealing with a different time-period which has not been correctly established on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zec, could you please clarify the issue as far as the month is concerned, whether we are talking about various events, and could you please make a distinction between what happened in Zvornik and what happened in Srebrenica and not put them in one question. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Bilbija --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm a little bit unclear because this in my question is related to the whole process of evacuations leading up to the witness's involvement. So that was my question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But okay --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: -- whether he was aware of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you should be clear that whether the witness is aware of what is described in this document as obstruction preceding the evacuation in which he participated, if that's your question, then we have clearly split the two events and the witness -- were you aware of what is described in this document as of an obstructive nature preceding the evacuation in which you participated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So were you aware that this was happening shortly before you got involved in this process?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the witness says he isn't aware of it, so therefore whether it was briefly before or long before is not a question which the witness could answer because he did not know that it happened. Next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I will move on, but I will then tender the video and the document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then could you take them one by one, first the video, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Video 65 ter number 22852A receives number P6959, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please check the 65 ter number. Is it really 22852?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Now the document which is on our screen, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 9358 receives number P6960, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Mr. Zec, is it the Prosecution's position that the video we looked at was depicting the evacuation in which this witness participated, that is, in April, or that it is depicting what happened in the month of March?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. So this is before his involvement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This is happening in March 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then of course the relevance of questions "is this what you saw," then it was not entirely clear, as a matter of fact. The witness said this was not what he saw, but it should have been made clear to him whether this was similar to what he saw because it's your position that it's not the moment that the witness was in Srebrenica and you should have clearly identified that in your questions. But it's clear now so let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In paragraph 17 you say that General Mladic ordered you to go to Srebrenica and to do the task given to you to the best of your abilities. And you also say in paragraph 18 that you promised to send a book to a doctor in Srebrenica through ICRC. So shortly after this and your visit to Srebrenica, General Mladic ordered to ban access to Srebrenica to all international organisations. Were you aware of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can we have a basis for this question in time and fact instead of just a generic question. There's a lot of time-period between after this witness left Srebrenica. I'd like to know the basis of this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ivetic, if there would have been a clear time-frame in paragraph 18 of the statement, then it would have made sense. But since there is not, the question is phrased in a rather general way and we can further -- oh, no, I'm sorry, 17 [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 17 does say April of 1993, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's right, and in the beginning of 18 it says during one of the pauses between the flights. Now let me just -- you're perfectly right, Mr. Ivetic. Apologies for that. Yes, are you aware at all of General Mladic ordering to ban access to Srebrenica to all international organisations after the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I am not aware of any such order. Are we going to talk about the book now and international organisations?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. We are talking about what Mr. Zec puts to you as questions. Mr. Zec, if you would have any specifics which might refresh the memory of the witness, then of course you have an opportunity to raise that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have 65 ter 31679. And this is a document issued by the intelligence and security department of the Drina Corps in May 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: It was sent to all Drina Corps units and it says: "Pursuant to the oral order of Lieutenant-General Ratko Mladic, commander of the VRS Main Staff, all convoys of UNPROFOR, the ICRC, and other international organisations are hereby banned from entering or leaving the territory of Srebrenica and Zepa." So the reality is, Mr. Bilbija, General Mladic banned access to Srebrenica about a month after your visit there; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear of this, what you've been saying, and I don't know how I could know about that in the first place. Why would I know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, whether you should or whether you could is a different matter. We are primarily interested in whether you knew; the answer is clearly no. Next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31679 receives number P6961, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: You told us in your statement about your contacts with General Mladic, starting from the time when you were in Croatia. And we saw some of it in the notebook that I showed to you earlier. Did you ever write to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Did you ever send him a letter and books?

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 02308.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And I'm going to show you a letter that was found in 2008 in premises belonging to General Mladic. The letter was found in an envelope which you can see on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have next page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So this is the other side of the envelope.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have next page in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So this is the letter and you -- if you look over, you will see that it refers to two books about bees that were sent through Stojan Maricic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have next page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Malcic, Malcic, Stojan Malcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you see at the end it says: "Yours, Simo." So I take it you recognise this letter, yes?

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And this is the letter that you sent to General Mladic, talking about the books that you sent to him; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we see the beginning of the letter, so in B/C/S we need page before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the letter you say: "Dear boss: "Our last meeting left a strong impression on me, I guess because we spent a lot of time alone together, undisturbed by these difficulties. I am happy to realise that your spirit has remained strong despite all the troubles ..." Mr. Bilbija, the troubles you were referring to were the indictment by this Tribunal and the arrest warrant for General Mladic; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The letter is dated the 2nd of September, 1996. It is correct, I did write it. Now I have to go back to this time when I wrote it to know -- but I don't think that - how do I put this? - yes, what did I write? "Trouble"? No, I don't think that I thought of The Hague Tribunal when I was referring to this trouble. When did that start, when was the indictment established? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This Tribunal has indicted General Mladic and requested his arrest in 1995. On 11 July 1996, following the failure to surrender the accused by the authorities of Serbia and Republika Srpska, the Trial Chamber issued an international arrest warrant, sent to all states and to the NATO forces in Bosnia, the IFOR. So that's the background of the indictment and the arrest warrant. So it's clear that what you said in this letter in September 1996, you were referring to the indictment and the arrest warrant; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I object to the form of the question. It's not at all clear. Counsel is presenting his version of events. The witness is entitled to testify as to what his recollections are of this letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now that's what we call a leading question and that's allowed in cross-examination. Could you tell us whether, as it was put to you by Mr. Zec, whether it was the arrest warrant that was on your mind when referring to "difficulties"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe just in part. I believe that what I meant by that was all the trouble that had befallen our people, him included. Would that do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if you say "in part," it means that that was included as well but not exclusively the difficulties and you described what other difficulties you refer to. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that you interpreted this properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Next question, please, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Towards the end of the letter - in B/C/S it's towards the end of this page - you say: "It is difficult to put everything into one short letter ... my family, friends, and everyone who would like ... to know how much they love and support you. I would also like to take this opportunity to send my greetings to the high-ranking ..." In B/C/S we should go to the next page. "... high-ranking Serbian officers in the Main Staff and convey to them my best wishes." And again, this is your support to a man indicted by this Tribunal; yes?

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: As you sit today in that witness box, do you still share the same feelings of love and support towards General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is why I'm sitting here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I tender this document. And I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 2308 receives number P6962, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you're on your feet. Is it still about the exhibit? No, no, then the exhibit is admitted into evidence. Mr. Ivetic, any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to focus now on the medevac evacuation that you participated in April of 1993 from Srebrenica. Mr. Zec asked about conditions in Srebrenica. Now, when you arrived, what kind of condition of the people did you expect going there and what kind of condition did you find there in terms of their nourishment?

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems to me that in the testimony up until now this has been dealt with fully, how I saw all of this in Srebrenica. My general impression was that it wasn't as terrible as it had been portrayed. As for this question regarding food, I am not in a position to answer because I did not really deal with that -- actually, in addition to the medical work, I asked my colleague about whether they received food supplies and so on, and he said they did. If you perhaps mean whether I saw people who were very thin, very skinny, no. They looked like others on all sides in this war. But this is just superficial, a superficial assessment on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand that. Earlier today at temporary transcript page 18, lines 2 through 4, in talking about the medical centre in Srebrenica you said: "His medical centre, objectively speaking, and as far as my impression goes, it just looked like any medical centre on the other side, on my side. It was nothing special." Could you please describe for us what other medical centres you were comparing when comparing the one in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said what you just said I said, I meant the health centres, the medical centres in similar small towns all over Bosnia and Herzegovina that I had the opportunity to go into up until that point. In war conditions, all of them were not well supplied and the hygienic conditions were difficult, but it did seem to work somehow. What I wanted to say was that when we entered the medical centre in Srebrenica, my colleague took me around, he showed me things. The patients' rooms had a number of empty beds and the reason for that was that those people who were lying in that bed at that point were at the football-pitch waiting to be boarded on to the helicopters. And all he said to me was that: Well, I wish you knew how crowded it could get here sometimes, which I knew, I knew what the situation was from other places when the wounded and the injured were being brought in in the middle of war. Is this sufficient?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Almost. Just one more clarification, sir. You said compared to other places that you had been, medical centres in similar small towns all over Bosnia. On whose territory were those medical centres located during the war that you're talking about, that you're comparing with Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were the hospital where I worked in Sokolac, the medical centre in Sokolac, the hospital in Pale, the hospital in Zica, in Kasindol, in Han Pijesak, in Srebrenica, I'm sorry -- Srebrenica, actually, I meant to say in Bratunac. I mean, it's clear that we are talking about Srebrenica already. The hospital in Bratunac, in Zvornik, the hospital in Bijeljina, the hospital in Brcko, Prijedor. And there were also a number of field hospitals too, but I assume that that is not part of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you've clarified sufficiently for us to get an idea of the comparison you're making. Now during your cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can I --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- take it that the parties agree that all the locations mentioned were Serb-controlled territory apart from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I definitely can stipulate that. I don't know about the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zec? I mean, the comparison is with what the witness found in Serb-controlled hospitals.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's my understanding, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you, Witness, could --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Da."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness has confirmed it so there's no need for stipulation further. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, during your cross-examination you mentioned -- or actually, you were asked about the lack of medical supplies in Srebrenica and you mentioned that you had been told about medical supplies being dropped from the air in Srebrenica. Did the doctor from Srebrenica tell you of any problems relating to those medical supplies dropped from the air which complicated the ability of their use for medical treatment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could you give us a page and line reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I did not go into this topic in my cross as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You did not ask about medical supplies in Srebrenica? Is that the Prosecution's position, that you did not ask about the lack of medical supplies in Srebrenica hospital?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I was thinking this was more focused on the way the air-drops, but I will leave it --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It goes directly towards an element that arose out of their cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- the availability of supplies to the hospital in Srebrenica, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- there are two elements -- as a matter of fact, there are three elements: Supplies, medical supplies, and the way in which they were transported to their destination. These are the three elements. Because I wanted to verify exactly what the witness has said, I asked you primarily, Mr. Ivetic, for a reference, and in view of the objection by Mr. Zec I would like --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Page 18 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Page 18 --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- lines 5 through 8, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 18, 5 to 8. And then in respect of the cross-examination you referred to is --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Beginning at temporary transcript 17, line 24, the witness is responding to Mr. Zec's question about lack of military supplies -- lack of medical supplies and what the doctor told him in Srebrenica. And now I'm going back to that to find out more information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. One second. Yes, that's 18. Then we have -- one second, please. Yes, you say starting at -- yes, at 24. There is about -- cross-examination dealt with medical supplies and being provided with things from Doctors Without Borders, and that there was some supplies from humanitarian air-drops. So both the type of support, being medical, and the transportation through air-drops was dealt with. Therefore, the objection by Mr. Zec is denied. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Doctor, did the doctor from Srebrenica tell you of any difficulties encountered with the humanitarian supplies from air-drops which complicated their use at the medical facility?

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the doctor told me -- well, we discussed a number of things but as far as air-drops are concerned, the doctor said that sometimes it would happen that the packages with medical supplies would unfortunately be opened by the population who were waiting for the packages. And the contents would be unpacked and that would destroy the sterile conditions of the material. And even though the day was difficult and tense and complicated, we did spend a long time together so we kind of even joked a little bit in that situation. I asked him: Why would they open sterile medical supplies? And the young colleague said: Well, you know, our people, they believed that in the packets that were marked with the red cross signs there were coffee and tobacco for the doctors. So the equipment, the material, was not destroyed completely. In a way he was describing anecdotes and he was showing me the supplies that he had that he was using. In spite of his quite moderate surgical experience, he came to Srebrenica after a short time which he spent specialising in pathology at the faculty of medicine in Sarajevo. So because of the circumstances, he was forced to provide surgical treatment, and in view of the situation, I believe that he did a very good job. I promised him a book then on war-time surgery, which I sent him later and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now I'd like to focus on the time-period that Mr. Zec was asking about, March of 1993, and I'd like to ask you, sir: Do you know if at that time, March of 1993, Srebrenica had been declared a safe area and been demilitarised or not, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did know at the time that this was something that was ongoing and that Srebrenica was declared a demilitarised safe area, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And can the -- is the Prosecution willing to stipulate that that occurred in April of 1993, the 19th of April, pursuant to UN Security Council Resolution number 824 -- pardon me, 819? And we can get back to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, I have one other area to ask about, that's the letter that was shown to you which you authored in September of 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you not waiting for an answer from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't think they can respond right away. I would like to give them time to research, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, at the same time we are close to the end of the testimony of this witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Agreed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- so therefore I think -- but I hardly could imagine that if there's a Security Council Resolution which deals with the matter, that there would be any dispute about it. So let's -- Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I refer to paragraph 72 of the indictment, which -- this has been dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. So there's a stipulation. There's no dispute about that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, in relation to the letter and the time-period and the troubles that General Mladic was undergoing, do you recall when it was that General Mladic was removed from his position by the Republika Srpska president in relation to your letter?

utterances.speaker: SIMO BILBIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Doctor, again, I thank you on behalf of my client, General Mladic, and the rest of the team for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that completes the re-direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Before I give an opportunity to Mr. Zec, I have one -- I'm puzzled by your observations about the sterility of the material that arrived, where the packages were opened by the local population because they thought there would be coffee in it. Do you remember your testimony in this respect? I'm just seeking to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I remember. Your Honour, this was not my observation. It was the observation of the local doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're right in correcting me. Now, I tried to understand how that works. If I open a package in which there is sterile material such as syringes, I take it, or whatever other surgical equipment, I have little knowledge about medical matters but usually they're packed in plastic, they are sealed so that you can see what the content is, whether it's syringes, whether it's anything else. So I wondered how by opening a package, seeing that there is medical equipment in there as I described, syringes, scalpels - how do you call them? - the lancets, for example, how would you then continue and further open that in the expectation that there would be coffee in it? I try to understand what happened. Do you have -- did he explain to you how the sterility was lost despite the fact that, as far as I know, it's usually discernible that it's medical equipment rather than coffee in those sealed elements.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I already said that this topic that we're talking about was something that made all of us laugh, me, him, everybody who was around us. It was my impression that that was the reason why he told it, because by that time we had already developed a very positive atmosphere in our mutual contact. He didn't say that everything that had been in the air-drop was unpacked and destroyed, he didn't say that. He just said that some things were opened quickly by those people, unpacked, and then it wouldn't be usable anymore. On the other hand, if we remember the video from earlier, you remember that they showed some moments where surgery was being carried out, we could see a little bit of that. The reporter who was speaking in the footage said that you could -- that the footage does not convey the stench of dirty sheets, wounds getting infected and so on. When you try to imagine that whole atmosphere, then the fact that two or three scalpels or a pack of sterile garments were unpacked is not that serious. Some things that we use that are unpacked -- once they're unpacked because they're no longer sterile, they cannot be used anymore according to our rules. However, in the situation which prevailed there, sometimes you had to work with things that were not 100 per cent sure, if you understand me. I hope that you understand me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I do understand you. One more question. We -- quite a lot of attention was paid to the March operation for evacuation. Now, we do understand you were not involved in that. Were you aware of that taking place and were you aware of which of your colleagues was involved in that evacuation? Because what we saw on our screens seemed, at least gave the impression, that patients were transported to the helicopters and -- are you -- do you know anything about this earlier attempt to evacuate which then apparently faced some trouble?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know about the earlier attempt at evacuation, so I'm surprised all the more because I was at the Main Staff hospital from where doctors would most probably have been recruited, doctors like myself. I didn't hear about that at all. I didn't hear about anything that we saw in the footage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that answers my question. Mr. Zec, any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, only to put on the record that the Security Council Resolution that Mr. Ivetic was referring to is Exhibit P22 in this case and also would like to put on the record that an agreement to demilitarise Srebrenica is P5 in this case. In paragraph 3 you will see there it's a discussion that two doctors from each side be involved in evacuations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That gives the documentary background of the events we heard about. Mr. Bilbija, this concludes your evidence. I would like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and for having the patience to stay over the weekend and conclude your testimony today. I wish you -- yes, for coming to The Hague I would like to thank you but also for having answered all the questions that were put to you, that were put to you by the parties, that were put to you by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it would be best to take the break now, although it's a little bit less than one hour, but to take the break and resume at quarter past 12.00. As usual, Mr. Mladic, being removed from the courtroom, is welcome again after the break. Mr. Ivetic or Mr. Lukic, it was confirmed to the Chamber that Mr. Mladic had an opportunity to follow the proceedings in the cell where he was through a video link. We take the break and resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber was informed that there was a preliminary matter to be raised by the Prosecution. Does it take a lot of time?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, and we could probably do it while the witness is being escorted in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I was just thinking about. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, during the testimony of Witness Corokalo on the -- specifically on the 18th of November, the witness was shown an article from "Vreme," V-r-e-m-e, "International."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: That was P6925 MFI'd. The Defence asked the Prosecution to stipulate that "Vreme" is published and distributed in Serbia. The Prosecution makes that stipulation. The Prosecution further notes that the article in question originated from "Vreme International." The Prosecution and Defence agree that Vreme --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'm trying to rush too much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are now at "Vreme International." Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: That "Vreme International" is published in Austria and circulated internationally. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I agree, that was the discussion I had with counsel from the Prosecution earlier this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
