utterances.text: Yes, then this stipulation is hereby on the record. We'll wait for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Stojanovic, I see the lectern is close to you, so you'll examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that you want to take the witness immediately to his statement. Perhaps you could already give the number so that everyone is prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The number is 1D01677.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Cvijic, good afternoon. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is handed out to you now. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Cvijic. Mr. Cvijic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Stojanovic. You'll find Mr. Stojanovic to your left. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, could you please repeat the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. 1D01677.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, good day. Could you please, as slowly as possible, tell us your correct first and last name.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO CVIJIC
utterances.text: My name is Zarko Cvijic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijic, at any point did you give a statement, a written statement, to General Mladic's Defence?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO CVIJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please have document that we referred to earlier, the 65 ter document 1D01677, in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you please look at the screen in front of you, where you will see the text and can you please tell us if the signature on this page is your signature?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO CVIJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at the last page of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijic, these two signatures that we see on the page and also the date that you can see on this page, are they written in your hand?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO CVIJIC
utterances.text: Yes, these are my signatures as well as the date, the 13th of June, 2014.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Today after you have given the solemn declaration that you will speak the truth here in this courtroom today, would you stand by your written statement and do you say that it is correct, truthful, and given according to your best recollection?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO CVIJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender the witness's statement into evidence, the Witness Cvijic Zarko, his statement which has the 65 ter number 1D01677.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that the witness understood your questions to be that the statement as written down reflects what he said, that it's truthful, and that he would give the same answers if -- in substance if questioned again. Is that what you confirm, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1677 receives number D833, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I assume that there are no objections. Admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave I would like to read the summary of the statement of Witness Cvijic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you explained to the witness the purpose of reading it, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness Zarko Cvijic, in July 1992, when he was 18 years old, went to do his regular military service, and after having been trained as a military policeman he was sent to the 65th Protection Regiment of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, where it was decided that he would be one of the escorts and members of the personal security detail of the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS, General Mladic. He spent a bit over a year carrying out these duties. In his statement he speaks about his personal observations and impressions about the nature and personality of General Mladic during the period while he was close to him and around him almost every day. He refers to a particular situation showing the attitude of General Mladic towards the non-Serb population; namely, he encountered a convoy of civilians who were moving from Srebrenica towards Tuzla escorted by blue helmets. Having noticed in the convoy a military-aged able-bodied man who was extremely frightened, he addressed him with a few ordinary questions, telling him not to be afraid and to continue his journey freely. He also showed his care and concern towards his subordinates in his personal attitude towards the witness too, asking that he should not be reassigned, which is what the witness wanted; rather, he kept him in his -- on his own security detail and soon afterwards sent him to train as an officer in Banja Luka. After completing his education, the witness assumed the rank of a second lieutenant and took over the duty of commander of a platoon of military police all the way up until the 13th of September, 1994, when he was wounded in both legs at the Nisici plateau. His assessment of General Mladic is that General Mladic is an honest man, an officer who never drew any advantage out of the war, and he also speaks of him as a very gentle man with a very stern exterior only. Your Honours, that would be the statement, and with your leave I would like to put a few questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Proceed as you suggest, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijic, during your proofing before you appeared before this Court, I've asked you and now I'm asking you once again to tell us more about your service. I will deal with this through questions. To the best of your recollection, when did you arrive in the 65th Regiment and until when were you part of General Mladic's security detail?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO CVIJIC
utterances.text: I arrived in the 65th Regiment sometime in 1992. That was the month of August 1992. After two months in the regiment, I was selected to provide security for General Mladic and I spent about a year on his security detail, that is to say, until the 1st of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From the 1st of September, 1993, you were sent out for continuing your education, so could you please tell the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, nothing in the first question or in its answer is not yet in the statement. So would you please put additional questions rather than to ask the same as we find already in the statement. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Then allow me just to draw the witness's attention to a paragraph for which I am actually asking this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you focus on paragraph 6 of your statement, D833 is its number now. Witness, in that paragraph of your statement you say that you served as General Mladic's security detail for a little over a year and my question is: Can you give us the date when you went out for your further education? And it was my understanding that that was the 1st of September, 1993. Thank you. Then yet again I'm going to indicate paragraph 14 of your statement. Please let us take a look at paragraph 14 of your statement. And you say there that you stayed for ten months in officers' training school, and then I'm asking you when you returned after your education to the 65th Regiment.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO CVIJIC
utterances.text: I completed the military school on the 30th of June, 1993. That's the exact date. And then I was returned to serve in the protection regiment again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat once again the date, the 30th of June which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And you said that you were sent out to school on the 1st of September?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm lost, Mr. Stojanovic. I thought the witness had served for a little over a year with General Mladic, from August 1992 to September 1993. Now he says he went to school again, leaving the service in June 1993, which is the time when he's supposed to be still with Mr. Mladic. Are you able to explain that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember the date when I became part of General Mladic's security detail. I don't remember the date in terms of the beginning. I do know that I stayed there until September 1993, roughly. I don't remember these dates. From September 1992 until the 30th of June, 1993, I trained at the military school in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to ask you to focus, please, on the time and tell us once again. You say in September 1992 you came to the 65th Protection Regiment, at the end of August/beginning of September?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO CVIJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You say that you went to school in September 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO CVIJIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How long did this education last, this training?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO CVIJIC
utterances.text: Ten months.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So when did you return then, what year was it?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO CVIJIC
utterances.text: The 30th of June, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what we wanted to clarify. And I'm not going to ask you about these dates any longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, by the way, I stand corrected, the beginning of the time was clear from the statement; however, the last moment or the -- when he left his duty as General Mladic's security was -- was not clear in the statement. So I stand corrected from my previous observation. Please proceed, and I think everything has been clarified by now as far as dates are concerned. So please put your next question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now I'd just like to ask you briefly about paragraph 10 of your statement. There's a reference to this convoy for transporting civilians. Could you tell the Chamber, to best of your recollection, where did this actually happen in physical terms?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO CVIJIC
utterances.text: In physical terms it was the area between Bratunac and Milici and then further on towards Sekovici at the crossroads to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know what the name of the place is, this crossroads or a settlement if there is one there?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO CVIJIC
utterances.text: I think it's Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to draw your attention to paragraph 13 of your statement. I would like to ask you to tell us how you experienced these reasons why General Mladic practically stopped the order of the commander of the 65th Regiment, Mr. Savcic, that is to say, stopped your transfer to Krajina, your reassignment?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO CVIJIC
utterances.text: Well, as that was happening straight away and when I was told that I should stay where I was, it wasn't very clear to me. But after a while General Mladic asked me to come to his office and he explained to me why it was that he did that. Primarily for my sake because I was young then and because of my personal safety. He said I was safer there than in any other unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijic, thank you for these answers. At this point in time we have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Ms. Edgerton, is the Prosecution ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijic, you'll now be cross-examined by Ms. Edgerton. You'll find her to your right. Ms. Edgerton is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Cvijic. Can you understand me?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO CVIJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just before we get in depth into the cross-examination, I just wanted to point out to my colleagues, it appears to be an error in the translation of paragraph 10 of the witness's statement that I noticed when I heard my colleague Mr. Stojanovic refer to the man mentioned in paragraph 10 as a military-aged man. Those words are missing from the English translation but they appear in the B/C/S. You may want to take care of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think then we need a corrected version of the translation to be uploaded if it's missing in the English because we might consult it later.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijic, I also want to ask you about the things you spoke about in paragraph 10 and paragraph 11 of your statement. And maybe it would be an idea while we do that for you to have that on the computer screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, we have it. Good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you said when you were there with General Mladic and you saw this convoy, you were in Serb-held territory probably around Konjevic Polje; right?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO CVIJIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that's the area of responsibility or that was the area of responsibility at the time of the Drina Corps; right?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO CVIJIC
utterances.text: I think the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Now, this convoy that you talked about that you said in your statement was brimming with civilian passengers, I want to ask you about that word. When you use that word "brimming," you mean that the convoy vehicles were packed to the point of overflowing, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO CVIJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Edgerton, the paragraph 11 that I have doesn't talk of civilian passengers, it just talks of passengers.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Ah, I -- indeed, at paragraph 10, first sentence, refers to the convoy being organised to transport civilians --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- from Srebrenica and Zepa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, these civilians in the convoy, they were fleeing horrible conditions in Srebrenica at that time, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO CVIJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Because the town of Srebrenica was just crammed with refugees at that time, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO CVIJIC
utterances.text: I think so. I wasn't there. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, do you know that they had no real food and that's one of the reasons why they were fleeing?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO CVIJIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that was one of the reasons too why they were moving out of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And they were also moving out of Srebrenica because their villages had been shelled by attacks from the VRS; right?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO CVIJIC
utterances.text: Probably. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in fact, Srebrenica had been shelled and was being shelled and that's one of the reasons why they were fleeing; right?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO CVIJIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was shelled or not. I was a soldier in military service. I don't know what was going on there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So are you saying that you don't know about the concerted military advance by forces of your army against the area of Srebrenica at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO CVIJIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But it was, Mr. Cvijic, exactly this advance, this offensive, that created the refugee situation that you just agreed to; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO CVIJIC
utterances.text: That is probably correct. I told you where I happened to be at that point in time and what happened. As for what the reason was for the withdrawal of those civilians, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this convoy that you talked about, you would remember that there were no men on the trucks, other than an extremely small number, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO CVIJIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were practically no men.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And Bosnian Serb army forces were checking every single one of those trucks as they crossed through the area looking for men of military age, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO CVIJIC
utterances.text: There was a check-point there. They were doing spot-checks. I don't know if they were looking for somebody or I don't know what they were doing, but in any case they were searching the buses and the trucks.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, in point of fact, they were looking for men of military -- men of fighting age, weren't they? Because there weren't supposed to be men of fighting age on any one of those trucks; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO CVIJIC
utterances.text: That is probably so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in fact, the men of fighting age in Srebrenica were being held back at the insistence of your Commander-in-Chief, General Mladic; that's what was going on, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO CVIJIC
utterances.text: No, nobody was being held back.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijic, you just agreed that there weren't supposed to be men of fighting age on any one of those trucks, and now you've just said nobody was being held back.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO CVIJIC
utterances.text: I told you nobody was being held back. The soldiers at the check-points - I don't know how - noticed one man among the women in the bus. And we happened to be there with General Mladic, I was there too. When we arrived, the convoy had already been stopped. Two soldiers brought the man that they had noticed, they brought him to General Mladic. I was standing nearby and I could hear every word. The man was frightened. He was saying that he wasn't the type for war, that he didn't carry weapons, and so on. And then General Mladic told him that he shouldn't be afraid, that he could go back to the bus from which he was taken, and he could continue with his journey. And that's exactly what the man did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijic, on the 26th of March, 1993, General Mladic attended a meeting with other military commanders. He attended a meeting with Wahlgren, he was with Morillon, and General Mladic struck a deal and the deal was that a convoy was to leave Srebrenica, evacuating women, children, and only some of the elderly. And that's at P346, English page 172 and B/C/S page 177. And, in fact, Mr. Cvijic, your own army recorded that there were only 48 men on that convoy. I'll let you have a look.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we see 65 ter number 09727.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And then I'll ask you a question. This is a Drina Corps command combat report to the VRS Main Staff on 29 March 1993. Now, can you read okay, Mr. Cvijic, because I want you to have a look at paragraph 4 in both languages. Now, that paragraph says: "Convoy of refugees, which left Srebrenica this morning, went to Tuzla via Bratunac, Zvornik, and Memici. The convoy consisted of 19 big vehicles and two small vehicles, which transported 2.140 people, of which 884 were women, 1.208 children, and 48 elderly men."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, Mr. Mladic, no speaking aloud. No speaking aloud. Your question, please, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijic, the men weren't allowed -- the men of military age weren't allowed to go out of Srebrenica because they were intended to be killed; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO CVIJIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 65 ter number 22229A. 22229A. We have it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: involving Drina Corps command officers, General Zivanovic and Colonel Prstojevic, and one of them, the second one, they made the conclusion based on the information they were hearing involved General Mladic. Now, have a look down at the second one, the second conversation on this list. It says: "... we learned the text of General Mladic's order that says: During the course of the day seize Potocari village (north of Srebrenica). Bosnian Serb forces around Srebrenica are to initiate attacks in order to enter the town today or tomorrow. Upon entering" the town "everyone who has weapons is to be killed. Civilians and wounded are to be taken out of the town ..." It's crystal clear from what you see was being discussed on the eve of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, no speaking aloud again. If you want to consult, please do it, but not audible for anyone in this courtroom. And then it's best to take off your earphones -- Mr. Mladic, if you take off your earphones, then you better hear what counsel are telling you. That's better. No, no further comments. No further comments. Mr. Mladic, you are -- you continue to speak aloud when I ordered you not to do so. You knew this morning what happened before. We turn into closed session for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijic, looking at that conversation that took place -- the summary of the conversation that took place at 9.30 in the morning on the 16th of April, it's crystal clear that what was being discussed was General Mladic's plan to enter the town and kill everybody who has a weapon; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. The quote is wrong. I point to page 61, line 25 of today's draft transcript, where the Prosecutor says, paraphrasing the alleged intercept, about the killing of militarily able-bodied men. In the original B/C/S text, it does not say that. With your leave, I would like to read what it says in the B/C/S version, which is completely contrary from what is quoted by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, if I read the document on the screen, it talks -- certainly in the second one but perhaps the first one as well, it is about men with weapons that are to be killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's not the same as men of military age.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, no. With respect, of course, Your Honour, it's not the same. I was simply asking the question at pages 61, lines 25, to 62, line 2, and it was later when I called up the document, I then asked a further question about -- relating to the text of the document. And you see that at page 63, lines -- although I'm listed as Mr. Elderkin, which is why I didn't see myself, page 63, lines 21 to page 64. And there I did, with respect, correctly paraphrase the document. The first point that my friend --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- has risen on is, in my submission, simply not an appropriate objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When putting the content to the witness in -- on page 63, Mr. Stojanovic, I think Ms. Edgerton quoted well that it was about men with weapons. If that is understood -- everyone, by the way, with weapons. If that is well understood, then do you still stick to your objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour, but it would be fair to the witness because the question was fairly long, it consisted of a number of elements which could possibly then lead the witness to be confused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Edgerton, I noticed that a couple of times indeed your questions are composite or least introduction to a question is composite. Would you please try to take matters step by step. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Understood, Your Honour. Perhaps I could abbreviate the question that I asked at page 63.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijic, do you see that this intercept discusses General Mladic's plan to enter Srebrenica and kill everybody who has a weapon?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO CVIJIC
utterances.text: That is what it says here, but I don't see that that was the objective.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment, Your Honours. Your Honours, I have nothing further. I'd simply like to tender the last two exhibits that I omitted to tender, the first one being 9727.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 9727 receives number P6963, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no objection to this document, and we stand by our earlier objection in relation to the intercept and that's in line with our objections to these types of documents. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6964 is marked for identification. Ms. Edgerton, if there are any further submissions on the matter, then I see that the first and the second intercept seems to be very similar, and I wondered whether -- although where one is at 9.00 and the other one is 9.30, to what extent there is overlap and to what extent these really are two different intercepts. Perhaps you could pay attention to that as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In our further submissions, absolutely. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I've forgotten, and my colleagues remind me of that, that P6963 is admitted into evidence. Ms. Edgerton, no further questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, any questions in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cvijic, during the year that you were in General Mladic's detail, did you at any point in time happen to be in a situation to see or to hear any order by General Mladic directed at subordinates that would refer to the killing of soldiers or civilians of the other side?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO CVIJIC
utterances.text: No, we were not able to hear or see any document or report or order.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever have the opportunity to hear the name or the last name of any high-ranking officer -- actually, the name of Lieutenant-Colonel Prstojevic?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO CVIJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear that officer's surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijic, you were asked about the convoy that you talked about. While you were with General Mladic at that particular occasion, was it ever said or was anyone directed that somebody should be taken off or separated from that convoy?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO CVIJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The check-point that you're talking about, was it manned by the army or the police?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO CVIJIC
utterances.text: I think that it was the military police of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to end with this question: Was that the period when combat was going around -- going on around Srebrenica and the surrounding area?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO CVIJIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In that period, the spring of 1993, were you aware of fierce fighting that was going on around Srebrenica, did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO CVIJIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware that any fighting was being conducted around that area, any fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Cvijic. The Defence of General Mladic thanks you and we have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO CVIJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Judge Moloto has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, do you know why during the check-point of the convoy that man was brought to Mr. Mladic by the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO CVIJIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps during the check they noticed that this man was youngish, perhaps he was, say, in his 40s, up to the age of 50. The reason why he was brought in, I don't know. That I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know why he was scared when he was talking to Mr. Mladic?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO CVIJIC
utterances.text: Well, the very idea of General Mladic. I don't know why he was frightened. Most of our troops were frightened when General Mladic would arrive for an inspection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Were you also frightened when Mr. Mladic came into your company?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO CVIJIC
utterances.text: Well, at first, during the first days of my service on the security detail of General Mladic, I didn't feel very comfortable when he was near me, when he would pass by me, when I stood there; however, as time went by, I noticed that he was a completely different person. I think that General Mladic is a good, honourable, sincere man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But in the first few days you were not scared, you were just uncomfortable?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO CVIJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And -- but this particular man who was being brought out of the convoy was scared?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO CVIJIC
utterances.text: That's what it looked like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And General Mladic said to him he mustn't be scared, he must go back into the bus?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO CVIJIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you say you don't understand why he was called to Mr. Mladic?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO CVIJIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, any further questions? If not, Mr. Cvijic, this concludes your testimony. I would like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague, a long way to The Hague, and for having answered all the questions that were put to you, put to you by the parties, put to you by the Bench, and wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I'm briefly addressing you. The events of this morning, of course, are not what we expect to happen. The next witness, if I understand well, will be examined by Mr. Zec in cross-examination. We have decided that Mr. Mladic can be present during the examination of that witness, but you'll understand in view of what happened this morning that one word spoken aloud will result in exactly the same as what happened this morning already twice. And I would like you to make that clear to Mr. Mladic. Of course he always -- if he can't control himself, he can waive his right to be present, but we do not allow anything as happened this morning and that should be clear to him. At the same time, we would accept that he is present during the examination of the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you want me to respond or only to transfer your message to Mr. Mladic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that is the first thing. Of course if you want to make any submissions on what happened this morning at any moment, of course you're free to do so, but at this moment I'm not seeking a response. At this moment I'm just informing you that the Chamber decided to allow Mr. Mladic to be present but under these very strict conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this morning Mr. Mladic only inquired, mentioning the name of my learned friend from the other side --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- whether he was from our area and he was asking Mr. Stojanovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- the personal -- that, first of all, is not the point. Second, any reference to a person who is functioning in a role in this courtroom to be discussed aloud with counsel is unacceptable, let that be perfectly clear. Speaking aloud in itself is not permitted by this Chamber, as you know and as Mr. Mladic knows, and often we have not taken immediate action if it nevertheless happens. But if it is about one of the persons in a role functioning in this courtroom, it certainly is inadmissible and that's the reason why we said we would consider what to do. And then Mr. Mladic continued to speak aloud where it was clear that him that he should not do that and those were the circumstances under which he was sent out the first time this morning. And I want you to make clear to Mr. Mladic that if he behaves in the same way, that the same will happen again, but that nevertheless we allow him to be present during the examination of the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break and we will resume at quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before the witness enters the courtroom, I do understand that the translation issue has been resolved which doesn't mean that -- of two documents which were associated exhibits where there were no translations but the translations are there, but I do understand that it was not the only reason why the Prosecution may object to admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So then the translation issue is dealt with and whatever remains, we'll hear about that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid that our side didn't understand what you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that there were two associated exhibits where no translations were uploaded which now are uploaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Which witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: With the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just check. It is the -- there are statements of March -- let me just have a look. Yes, there were statements of 2006 and there was a -- two statements of 2006, March and May, which were announced as associated exhibits where there were no translations earlier uploaded, but as I understand they are uploaded now. That was what I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I didn't know about the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Another matter is --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- the objections at all, we were not aware, so that is why we did not understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, that one of the members of Chambers staff was in touch with Defence last Friday regarding the translations and noted that they both now are uploaded, so it was not an objection by the Prosecution but it was noticed by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It was noticed by the Prosecution in the response to your 92 ter motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I missed that, I made a mistake. But at least it was an issue and it has been resolved, at least that issue, not everything yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just -- is there anything -- I would have expected the witness to enter the courtroom already for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Milojica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Milojica. Mr. Milojica, you'll first be examined by Mr. Lukic. You find Mr. Lukic to your left. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. And could the usher assist in having the earphones rightly on -- if you put them on the top of your head, they don't fall off. Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Milojica.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILOJICA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For the record, could you please slowly state your name and surname.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILOJICA
utterances.text: My name is Ratko Milojica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 65 ter 1D4968 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milojica, did you provide a statement to the members of the Defence team of Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILOJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we see the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Milojica, on this document can you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILOJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Whose signature is that before you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILOJICA
utterances.text: My own.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Have you checked whether this statement correctly reflects what you said to the members of Mr. Karadzic's Defence?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILOJICA
utterances.text: Yes, my statement.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to come closer to the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you please come closer to the microphone so that the interpreters can hear you better. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just to check where I stopped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether the witness has given -- whether it's -- the statement correctly reflects what he said. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is contained in this statement, is it all correct and true, Mr. Milojica?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILOJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will have to pause a bit between question and answer so that we would make it possible for the interpreters to interpret what we're saying into English and French. If I were to put the same questions to you today, as the members of the Karadzic Defence did and you provided answers to those questions, would your answers be the same today?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILOJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At this moment, Your Honours, we would offer this statement into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D4968 receives number D834, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will read the statement summary of this witness and I will not have questions for this witness. Ratko Milojica was a member of the VRS and he has deployed -- he was deployed in the 343 Prijedor Motorised Brigade. On the 22nd of May, 1992, he was on leave and went to Prijedor with his neighbour Rade Lukic and half-brother Radovan Milojica to return to the army. However, they were told that they were not required for two more days and to return home. The three men were picked up in a car driven by Milenko Lulic with Sinisa Mijatovic and Nedjeljko Antunovic as passengers. They planned to travel to Ljubija via Hambarine. Lulic and Mijatovic just responded to a call-up. Two out of six passengers had their weapons with them. Their military equipment was in the boot of the car. At the check-point in Hambarine, Ratko Milojica noted that there was an anti-tank hedgehog barriers, sandbags, which created a parapet on which an M53 light machine-gun was placed with a civilian standing next to it. All the people at the check-point were armed. The men in the car were asked for their identity papers and the boot of the car was searched. The uniforms in the boot of the car were thrown on the ground, stamped upon; their military IDs and rifles were taken, and at this point, fire from the light machine-gun was opened upon them and the other people at the check-point joined in. They fired for approximately five minutes. Milenko Lulic attempted to run from the check-point but was shot as he did so. The others remained in the car whilst being shot at but were then ordered to get out of the car. Following this, the men were mistreated, kicked, threatened at knife point and shot at. At one point of time Mr. Milojica lost his consciousness. He was transported to Prijedor by the ambulance but has no recollection of that. Later he found out that Radovan Milojica and Rade Lukic were killed at that check-point and that other three men had survived but were all seriously wounded in the attack. To summarise, this was an attack on the civilian car at Hambarine check-point in connection with Prijedor municipality. That was a statement summary, Your Honours, and I don't have questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Zec, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Milojica, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Zec. You'll find him to your right. Mr. Zec is counsel for the Prosecution. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Milojica.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILOJICA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: On the night of 7 to 8 November 1992, the local Catholic priest of Donja Ravska near Prijedor, Ivan Grgic, was murdered; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILOJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Soldiers came to the priest's house, grabbed him, dragged him to Ljubija mine, shot him, and left his body there; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILOJICA
utterances.text: It's not that soldiers came and grabbed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In fact, you were one of these soldiers; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILOJICA
utterances.text: Yes, I was in the vehicle. I was going to the doctor's. Ivica Pavlovic got him out and said that he was supposed to bring him to the command. That's what I said in my first statement, too, when I was here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And you blamed Ivica Pavlovic, a local Croat, for this murder; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILOJICA
utterances.text: It's not that I blamed him. He himself admitted that he had done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Ivica Pavlovic died shortly after he confessed to the murder; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILOJICA
utterances.text: Yes, he allegedly committed suicide.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: You were never tried for this murder; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILOJICA
utterances.text: Well, the lawyer explained to me that I gave this statement as a suspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: But you never were -- you were never tried? There was never a trial for this murder; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILOJICA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Are you now saying that you were tried for this murder? Because that's not what you said last time when you were here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember that there was a trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Page 80, line 13 to 15, there was a question and it was answered: "You were never tried? There was never a trial for this murder; correct?" "No." So I don't see the point of the next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Zec, I do understand that when you asked the witness whether he was never tried, he said "no," which of course is always a bit of a dubious -- "no, there was no trial"; or "no, I was tried." So therefore, Mr. Lukic, that creates always the confusion and should be verified such an answer. And just now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And the "no" can also refer to "correct."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell us, was there ever a trial -- were you ever tried for this murder, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zec, that makes the next question superfluous.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And you said that you were interviewed about this murder by the investigative judge of the Banja Luka military court. That was in 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILOJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I just wondered, following the questions - and I'm addressing you as well, Mr. Zec - whether a 90(E) warning would be appropriate?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And my apologies for that. I should have said that at the beginning, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I'll read to you Rule 90(E) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, which is: "A witness may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate the witness. The Chamber may, however, compel the witness to answer the question. Testimony compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against the witness for any offence other than false testimony." Which means that if a truthful answer would tend to incriminate yourself, you may ask that you don't have to answer that question. That should be clear to you because you're talking about -- at least the questions are about being involved in a murder. That's the reason why I bring this to your attention. Mr. Zec, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Can we have 65 ter 31697 on the screen. And this is a record of interview dated 21 October 1993. Can we focus at the lower part of the first page in B/C/S and in English it's 2 -- page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Milojica, you see your name and the last name. Towards the bottom it says: "Ratko Milojica, Ratko, son of Mile and Milka Milojica." Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILOJICA
utterances.text: I see that here, here on the left; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And below that there's a signature. That's your signature; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILOJICA
utterances.text: Yes, my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we now turn to page 3 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And it says: "Between 7 and October -- between 7 and 8 November 1992, Boro Milojica, my cousin, Ranko Karan, aka Roca, and I were in my house in the village of Tisova. We were sitting and drinking a little and then we agreed to go to the priest, Ivan Grgic, in Gornja Ravska. We knew, because it was publicly discussed, that the priest had been the main supplier of weapons for the HDZ and that he had arranged for Croats to go over to the Croatian army. We wanted to intimidate him and make him tell us where he was hiding the weapons and to whom he had given them. It was about 24 hours when we set off from my house in a ... car driven by Boro Milojica. On the way to Gornja Ravska we met Ivica Pavlovic who joined us when we told him where we were going." This is what we told the investigative judge. Do you accept this part?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILOJICA
utterances.text: I do not accept that because I've already stated at that trial that this is not my statement. It is my signature, but when they were asking me questions, they were typing something, writing something. I didn't understand any of this. We were all threatened. We were threatened to be court-martialed, this and that, and it's obvious that I never even read this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I just read to you what is recorded. Do you accept that this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zec, what do you mean by "do you accept that"? Because it could be that: Do you accept that this is how it is recorded? Or do you mean: Do you accept that this is what you said? The witness has answered that question. So the acceptance is an unclear -- results in an unclear question. Could you please rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So as you sit now in that chair, is this your memory as to what happened that night? Before you set to go to the priest's house?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILOJICA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Then tell us, what is your memory now?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILOJICA
utterances.text: Well, I said that during the first trial here, that I had set out to the doctor's and -- towards Ljubija and that Pavlovic Ivica is someone we encountered on the way and he said that he had to bring in the priest, that he received orders from the command telling him that he had to bring him in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I will now read you the second paragraph and tell me whether you agree with the second portion. "Upon arrival in Donja Ravska we drove the car past" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zec, it reads "Gornja Ravska," not "Donja."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: "Upon arrival in Gornja Ravska, we drove the car past the priest's house. Boro, Ivica, and Roca went back to the priest's house, and I stayed by the car. When I saw that the priest had opened the door, I joined them and we all entered the house. We sat down with the priest and asked him where the weapons were and where he had put them. Boro Milojica asked the questions. The priest Grgic kept saying he knew nothing. Then Ranko Karan searched the priest's house and found 300 Deutschemarks and 100 Swiss francs under the pillow ..." So do you accept this portion, that this is what you told the investigative judge in 1993?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILOJICA
utterances.text: No, I do not accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I will go on. "After that we told the priest Grgic to come with us, saying that we were taking him to Ljubija for questioning. We wanted to frighten him so that he would tell us who his collaborators were who supplied him with weapons. When we arrived at the Ljubija mine, we went to Kipe - a part of the Ljubija mine - and took the priest out of the car. Roca ordered him to lie down, and when he did Roca asked him: 'Where are the weapons?' and hit him twice. Then the priest said: 'I don't know - I will tell you' ..." Do you accept this part as to what happened when you got the priest at the Ljubija mine?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zec, the previous portion you asked the witness whether this is what he said. Now -- and let's try to avoid whatever confusion, now you're asking whether this is what happened. Did you -- isn't the proper order to first ask the witness whether this is what he said or not and then perhaps follow-up with another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Milojica, you heard Judge Orie's question. So is this you what you said to the investigative judge in 1993?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILOJICA
utterances.text: No, I did not state that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zec, I'm looking at the clock. I know that we are in the middle of a quotation, but nevertheless, I think we should adjourn for the day because otherwise we might go well beyond our time-limits. Witness, we'll adjourn for the day and we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30 in this same courtroom, but before you leave I instruct you that you should not speak with anyone or communicate in whatever way with whomever about your testimony, whether that is testimony you've given today or whether that's testimony still to be given tomorrow. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you may follow the usher and we would like to see you back tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day and we'll resume tomorrow, Tuesday, the 2nd of December, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 2nd day of December, 2014, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.16 p.m.,
